brief: The New York Times now bars photographers from *Photoshop 2027*, reported PetaPixel, over its new AI tools.
Photographers signed a statement against Australia's plans to loosen *copyright* for AI training.
Viewers accuse Fincher's new Netflix film of *AI visuals*; the claim is unproven.
Creators say AI *reskins* of their viral videos are circulating with synthetic characters.
Try this week: *Magic Layers* to rescue flat files, and Photoshop's Remove tool for shadows and reflections.

items.title: New York Times bars photographers from using Photoshop 2027
items.summary:
PetaPixel reported on November 24 that The New York Times prohibits its photographers from using Photoshop 2027 (version 28.0.0). PetaPixel notes the release added many AI-powered editing features, including generative tools, and that photojournalists are taking note of the heavier focus on generative AI. I could not open the full article, so the exact wording of the Times' rule and its scope are not confirmed here. Creative Bloq also published a column on November 26 on how Adobe might win back trust after the ban.

For a designer this is a reminder that editorial clients are drawing hard lines about which tools touch their images. If you deliver to news or magazine clients, ask early what their AI policy covers: generative fill, expand, relight, or any edit. Keep a plain list of which tools you used on each file; it is cheap to do and saves a dispute later.

items.title: Photographers sign statement against Australia's AI copyright plans
items.summary:
PetaPixel reported on November 25 that photographers have signed a statement protesting the Australian government's plans to weaken copyright law to benefit AI companies. The report's details were not readable to me beyond that summary, so the number of signers and the specific proposal are not confirmed here. For background, Australia's attorney-general ruled out a text-and-data-mining exception in October 2025, so this appears to be a fresh round of the debate.

Why it matters: the rules on training data decide whether the people who made the images behind AI tools get asked or paid. If you sell illustration, photography or type, watch how this settles, because the same arguments are running in the US, UK and EU. It is also a prompt to check the licence terms on any stock or AI-made asset you put in client work.

items.title: Google patent describes feeds of personalized AI-made video and ads
items.summary:
The Verge reported on November 25 that Google filed a patent last May, published last week, for a system called My Channel. It would use a person's demographic data and viewing history to write prompts for an AI model that generates personalized videos and advertisements. The patent has been rejected, but Google could appeal or resubmit an amended version. A patent is not a product, and Google has announced no launch.

The idea matters to anyone making ads and social content: if feeds can be generated per viewer, the single hero campaign gives way to endless variants. Treat it as a signal to keep your brand system strict, since templates, type and color rules are what hold up when content is produced at scale.

items.title: Fincher's new Netflix film is accused of AI visuals; no confirmation yet
items.summary:
The Verge reported on November 24 that early screenings of David Fincher's The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, a sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood starring Brad Pitt, led viewers to claim on social media that the film has uncanny, inconsistent visuals and looks like AI slop. The film premiered November 25. Netflix has reportedly bought InterPositive, an AI post-production company, and one report links Fincher to its tools, but that connection is an inference and I found no confirmation from Netflix or Fincher.

The lesson for creatives is about perception: audiences now hunt for AI tells, and suspicion alone can damage a project. If you use AI in client work, decide in advance what you will disclose, and check generated elements closely for inconsistent hands, text and repeated details before delivery.

items.title: Creators say AI characters are replacing them in copies of their viral videos
items.summary:
PetaPixel reported on November 25 that content creators are finding AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical except that they have been swapped for AI-generated characters. The full article was not readable to me, so platforms, examples and numbers are not confirmed here.

If your social content is distinctive, expect it to be copied this way. Keep dated source files and drafts as proof of authorship, put recognizable branding in the frame and not only in an overlay, and check the platform's reporting tools for impersonation before you need them.

items.title: Turn a flat PNG or JPG into editable layers with Canva Magic Layers
items.summary:
Canva's help center says Magic Layers splits a flat image into separate editable elements, keeping the layout and hierarchy. In a design, upload the image, select it, choose Edit in the toolbar, then Magic Layers; from the homepage you can start from the Magic Layers tile. It takes single-page PNG or JPG files up to 5000px on the longest edge, and works best on graphics, illustrations and stylized visuals; photos may not separate cleanly. Canva's page did not state plan requirements in what I read, so check whether your plan includes it.

Try it on an old client carousel slide or a flattened social post when the source file is lost: split it, swap the text, move the elements, and re-export in a new size. Always review the layer edges before sending.

items.title: Remove an object and its shadow and reflection in Photoshop 28
items.summary:
CG Channel reports that Photoshop 28.0 adds "Remove related elements" to the Remove tool. It deletes the object and the traces it left, such as shadows, reflections, smoke, steam, water ripples and footprints. It runs online and uses generative credits; CG Channel notes single-app Photoshop plans include 25 free credits a month, with more through a separate Firefly subscription, so it is a paid tool. The article was updated on October 12, 2026.

Use it to clean product photos and mockup backgrounds before they go into a brand deck or social post. Work on a duplicate layer, check the fill edges at 100% zoom, and tell clients with strict AI rules (see the New York Times story above) that the tool is generative.

items.title: Keep a carousel's look consistent with style references in Firefly Boards
items.summary:
Adobe's help pages say Firefly Boards lets you use an image on the canvas as a guide for new images: "Use as style references" matches the style and "Use as composition reference" matches layout and structure. You can also remix two or more selected images, arrange them in rows or a mosaic, and group them into artboards. Boards is part of Adobe Firefly; Adobe's pages I read did not list a plan, and generation likely uses credits, so check your plan.

A practical test: pick one approved slide or brand image, set it as the style reference, and generate the remaining visuals for a five-slide carousel. Then move the results into Photoshop or Canva and set the type yourself, since you control the type and the brand system best.
